title: What If You Were Born as Al Capone? | Prohibition Chicago

paras: If you were born as Al Capone, you'd run a whole city by twenty-six.
Walk out of a restaurant that just took a thousand bullets.
And the thing that finally takes you down?
Not a gun.
A tax form.
But right now?
You're a baby in Brooklyn.
No money. No gang. Not even a scar.
You're born Alphonse Capone, in January 1899, a few blocks from the Brooklyn Navy Yard.
Your parents came over from Italy six years ago with almost nothing.
Your dad, Gabriele, is a barber.
All day, he stands with a razor in his hand, careful and steady, so nine kids can eat.
Remember that razor.
Your mom, Teresa, sews to bring in a little more.
You're the fourth of those nine kids.
Your big brothers are Vincenzo, Ralph and Frank.
And you?
You're good at school.
Until you aren't.
You're fourteen, in the sixth grade.
A teacher hits you.
You hit her back.
The principal beats you, and you never go back to school again.
Not one day.
Your classroom is the street now.
And on your street, there's a man who doesn't look like the others.
His name is Johnny Torrio.
He doesn't drink. He doesn't swear. He goes home to his wife every night.
He wears a clean, quiet suit.
And he runs gambling, loans and worse out of a building near your house.
You start running errands for him.
Torrio teaches you the most important rule in his world.
Don't be a thug.
Be a businessman.
Remember that suit.
By sixteen, you're in the Five Points gang.
You work in a candy store, a bowling alley, a factory cutting paper.
None of it sticks.
Then Torrio sends you to his friend Frankie Yale, who owns a rough bar on Coney Island called the Harvard Inn.
You're the bartender.
And the bouncer.
One night in 1917, a young woman walks in with her brother.
You lean over and say something crude about her.
Loud enough for him to hear.
Her brother is Frank Galluccio.
He tells you to apologize.
You don't.
He pulls a blade.
Three cuts, across the left side of your face.
Remember your dad's razor?
Careful. Steady. Feeding nine kids.
This one feeds nothing.
The scars give you a name you'll hate for the rest of your life.
Scarface.
Later, you tell people you got them fighting in the war in France.
You were never in the army.
Not for one minute.
And Frank Galluccio?
Yale makes you apologize to him.
Years later, you hire him as your bodyguard.
You meet a quiet Irish girl named Mae Coughlin.
In December 1918, she has your son.
Albert Francis. You call him Sonny.
Weeks later, you marry her.
Sonny gets a terrible ear infection.
The doctors have to operate on his skull.
He'll be partly deaf for the rest of his life.
And for the rest of your life, he's the one person you can never say no to.
You get an honest job, keeping the books for a construction company in Baltimore.
You're good with numbers.
Really good.
Remember that too.
Then, in November 1920, your dad drops dead of a heart attack.
He's fifty-five.
And a letter arrives from Chicago.
It's Torrio.
He has a job for you.
You get to Chicago at the perfect moment.
America has just made beer, wine and whiskey illegal.
Prohibition.
But people don't stop drinking.
They just stop paying taxes on it.
And Torrio sees it before anyone.
Hidden bars called speakeasies.
Secret breweries.
Trucks of beer moving at night with cops paid to look away.
You're his right hand.
Your business card says Alphonse Capone, second-hand furniture dealer.
In 1924, you help Torrio take over a whole town next to Chicago called Cicero.
On election day, your men stand at the polls with guns.
The police come, and in the gunfight, they kill your big brother Frank.
He's still in his twenties.
Then your side kills the boss of the rival North Side gang, in his own flower shop.
And the North Side comes for revenge.
In January 1925, they shoot Torrio outside his home.
Again and again.
Somehow, he lives.
But when he gets out of the hospital, he's done.
He hands you everything.
The bars. The breweries. The cops. The war.
You're twenty-six years old.
And Chicago is yours.
Now they call you the Big Fella.
You wear bright suits, a diamond ring, a pearl-grey hat.
You ride in an armored car.
You pay off cops, judges, even the mayor's people.
By some guesses, your business brings in a hundred million dollars a year.
Nobody really knows.
You never write it down where anyone can see.
September 1926.
You're having lunch in Cicero, at the Hawthorne restaurant.
Outside, a line of cars rolls slowly down the street.
Then the guns open up.
Machine guns, shotguns, pistols.
More than a thousand rounds, into the windows, the walls, the cars outside.
Your bodyguard, Frankie Rio, throws you to the floor and lies on top of you.
When it stops, you stand up.
You're not even scratched.
A woman sitting in a car outside isn't so lucky.
Glass hits her eye.
You pay thousands of dollars for her doctors.
To the papers, you're a monster.
To half of Chicago, you're Robin Hood.
Quick pause.
A lot of you asked for gangsters, so here's the biggest one of all.
Who should live next? Leave a name in the comments.
And if you want a new life every few days, subscribe.
By 1929, you've bought a mansion on an island in Miami.
That's where you are on February fourteenth.
Valentine's Day.
Back in Chicago, in a garage on North Clark Street, seven men from the North Side gang are waiting for a delivery.
A police car pulls up.
Men in police uniforms get out.
They line the seven men up against the wall.
And they shoot them all.
The man they really wanted, the North Side boss Bugs Moran, was running late.
He saw the police car and walked away.
Nobody is ever charged.
Nobody agrees on who planned it.
But everyone in America thinks they know.
And suddenly, Robin Hood isn't funny anymore.
The President himself wants you gone.
The story goes that Herbert Hoover keeps asking his people the same question.
Have you got that fellow Capone yet?
A young agent named Eliot Ness rams through your brewery doors with a truck.
It's great for the newspapers.
But it's not what gets you.
What gets you is a book.
A ledger, found in an old raid on one of your gambling houses.
Columns of numbers. Profits.
And money paid out to someone called Al.
Remember those books you kept in Baltimore?
You never kept your own.
Not on paper. Not for the government.
You have never filed a tax return in your life.
In 1930, the Great Depression hits.
You open a soup kitchen in Chicago and feed thousands of people for free.
It doesn't help.
In October 1931, you go on trial for tax evasion.
Your men have bribed the jury.
So on the first morning, the judge quietly swaps it for a jury from a different trial.
Guilty.
Eleven years.
You're thirty-two.
Seven years after Chicago became yours, it's over.
In the Atlanta prison, you still live like a king.
Rugs. Cash. Favors.
So in 1934, they put you on a train in chains, and send you to a brand-new prison on an island in San Francisco Bay.
Alcatraz.
Here, you're not the Big Fella.
You're prisoner eighty-five.
You mop floors.
You play banjo in the prison band.
Another prisoner stabs you with a pair of scissors.
You live.
But something else is killing you.
Years ago, in your Brooklyn days, you caught syphilis.
You never treated it.
And now it's in your brain.
You start talking to people who aren't there.
Some days you don't know where you are.
In November 1939, they let you go.
You go home to the mansion in Miami.
Mae is there. Sonny is there.
The man who ran Chicago now spends his days fishing off the dock and walking by the pool in his pajamas.
A doctor says your mind is like a twelve-year-old's.
People around you say you give orders to men who aren't in the room.
Men who've been dead for years.
In January 1947, you have a stroke.
Then pneumonia.
On January twenty-fifth, with your family around you, you die.
You're forty-eight.
You were a barber's son who swapped the razor for a blade.
You lost your brother Frank, your freedom, and in the end, your mind.
You survived a thousand bullets, a gang war and the whole Chicago police.
But Torrio's lesson came true in a way he never meant.
You wanted to be a businessman.
And you went down like one.
Over a tax form.
You always said you were just giving people what they wanted.
So tell me.
Was Al Capone a businessman, or a monster?
